what_its_for: Etodolac is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to relieve pain, swelling, and stiffness caused by arthritis (including osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis). It can also be used for general pain relief.
how_to_take: Take etodolac by mouth with a full glass of water (8 ounces). To help prevent an upset stomach, take it with food, milk, or an antacid. Do not lie down for at least 10 minutes after taking it. Swallow extended-release tablets (XL) whole — do not crush, chew, or break them. Take this medicine at the same time(s) each day to help you remember.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your condition. For regular tablets or capsules, the usual adult dose for pain is 200–400 mg every 6 to 8 hours as needed, not exceeding 1,000 mg per day. For arthritis, the usual dose is 300–500 mg two to three times daily, or 400–1,000 mg once daily for extended-release tablets, not exceeding 1,200 mg per day. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and never take more than prescribed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store etodolac at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C–25°C). Keep it away from heat, light, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of unused or expired medication properly — ask your pharmacist about medication take-back programs.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking etodolac, as it increases your risk of stomach bleeding. Do not take aspirin or other NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen or naproxen) unless your doctor tells you it is okay. Avoid smoking, as it can worsen stomach problems. Be careful when driving or doing tasks that require alertness, as etodolac may cause dizziness. Avoid prolonged sun exposure, as NSAIDs can occasionally increase sun sensitivity.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice: black, tarry, or bloody stools; vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds; chest pain, shortness of breath, sudden weakness, or slurred speech (signs of heart attack or stroke); swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; severe skin rash, blistering, or peeling; yellowing of the skin or eyes (signs of liver problems); rapid weight gain or swelling in your legs or ankles; decreased or no urination; or severe stomach pain. Also call your doctor if you develop new or worsening heartburn, stomach pain, or changes in your vision.
when_it_works: For pain relief, etodolac may start working within 30 minutes to 1 hour after your first dose. For arthritis symptoms like swelling and stiffness, it may take a few days to a couple of weeks of regular use before you notice the full benefit. Keep taking it as prescribed even if you feel better, and do not stop without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and over): Use with extra caution. Older people have a higher risk of stomach bleeding, kidney problems, and heart side effects. The lowest effective dose should be used for the shortest time possible. Pregnancy: Do NOT use etodolac during the last 3 months (third trimester) of pregnancy as it can harm the unborn baby. Consult your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Talk to your doctor before using etodolac while breastfeeding. Kidney or liver disease: Use with caution and close monitoring; dose adjustments may be needed. Children: Safety and effectiveness in children have not been fully established; use only if directed by a doctor.
